Now read the question.
Many people feel nervous or afraid of visiting the dentist.
But as dentists, there are a few simple things we can do to help our patients overcome their
fear.
First is to be open to having potential patients come and visit the surgery, meet the receptionist
and you, the dentist, in order to get a feel for the environment. If possible, make time
to talk with anxious patients about what their fears are.
The next tip is to have your receptionist advise anxious or nervous patients to pick
an appointment time early in the morning so they have less time to dwell on their feelings
about the appointment. Speaking of this first appointment, it should be a checkup, not a
treatment as this will give the patient time to get comfortable with you and your staff.
During this checkup you may want to discuss with patients a sign to signal that they need a
break and that they want you to stop. It should be something simple like pointing your finger,
this will help the patient feel more in control of the situation. So some types of patients that
may be anxious or fearful of the dentist are.

So, hello Dr Stalings. It is nice to have you here today to talk about a topic that
has captured the attention of the nation, the plight of junior doctors in our national
healthcare system.
Yes, it is very serious problem that has the potential to have a negative long-term effect
on healthcare in our country.
So tell me, what you see is the crux of the problem.
Hmm, it is definitely a complex problem.
So coming to just one cause is not possible.
But what I would say is that morale among junior doctors in our country is at an all-time
low, which explains why resignations are rising.
But also, sadly, why suicide among doctors is such a huge problem.
Well, our resigning is one thing, but suicide is another matter altogether.
Why do you think this is such a problem among doctors?
It is mostly due to the pressures of our work.
I mean, people who have trained to be doctors are incredibly committed and passionate about
what they do.
So there is a tendency to try work through the pressure until, of course, it becomes too
much.
Just a statistic that can help to illustrate the severity of the situation.
Female doctors are reported to be four times more likely to die by suicide compared to
females in the general population.
What do you think needs to be done to start to tackle this problem?
Well the first thing is to acknowledge the problem.
One colleague recently wrote an interesting post in our prominent journal and her main
point was that we need to stop the culture of shame that is part of the culture of our
national healthcare system and come together to create safe spaces for staff to learn and
reflect together.
It is somewhat ironic that it is our life's work to take care of others but we do not
have structures in place to ensure the well-being of all staff.
So few moments ago you mentioned resignations. What do you think would lead a doctor who,
as you stated, starts off so full of enthusiasm for the profession to resign?
Well, in my experience, the number one reason is professional passivity. You come full of
energy and enthusiasm and you think you can change things for the better. But then you
confront the system. You try to raise issues are concerned and are met with
walls. Eventually being ignored leads to disengagement. I see I'd never thought
of that so what do you think can be done to solve this particular problem? Well
to remedy this junior doctors must be encouraged and enabled to be involved
in professional development opportunities such as leadership and
research. Many are not permitted to be involved in these activities as the
focuses on the provision of services. While I understand there is a shortage of doctors,
such as GPs, forcing junior doctors to only focus on service provision is short-sighted.
Research by leading organisations has shown how important flexibility is in maintaining
doctors' well-being. In addition, developing non-clinical skills is of utmost importance for
the future of training and healthcare as a whole. Providing junior doctors with the opportunity
to develop leadership and reshut skills could definitely improve trainee satisfaction
and therefore improve retention and recruitment rates.
So is it all gloom and doom for junior doctors or is there some hope?
No, no, of course there is some hope. In fact, things are on the cusp of improving.
Junior doctors are coming together to advocate for quality improvement and for learning about
the managerial side of the job so that beneficial changes can be made. For example,
a focus group of junior doctors show that some places of work are putting into place new ways
of developing ideas, such as through regular meetings with the medical and managerial teams
to highlight problems and work together to resolve them. There are also some efforts that while well
intentioned need to be reviewed to make sure that they are effective as they can be. For example,
the mandatory e-learning modules need to be reviewed to look for ways that they can be made
more flexible and for ways that doctors can have more of a role in shaping their own training.
This would mean that junior doctors would engage more and stay in posts that are beneficial to
their career and it would also allow for other more practical activities such as discussing
difficult cases to be valued as learning activities. What about mentoring schemes? Are they viewed
favorably by junior doctors? Oh yes, they certainly are. I was recently part of a mentoring scheme
and all the mentees and mentors found it very useful in their professional practice.
In particular, mentees said it helped them to feel more engaged and that it was beneficial for their health.

So, well, we are all here today as part of a worldwide response to a new virus, a virus
that belongs to the large family of viruses known as coronaviruses.
Just to give us some background, before getting into the details of the current outbreak,
coronaviruses are generally zoonotic, meaning they are transmitted between animals and people.
Rarely, animal coronaviruses can infect people and then spread between people, such as with
SARS, MERS and now the new virus, officially named SARS-CoV-2.
So the first coronavirus outbreak that I'm going to discuss is SARS, which was first
reported in Asia in early 2003.
SARS stands for severe acute respiratory syndrome.
The illness then went on to spread to more than two dozen countries in North America,
South America, Europe and Asia before the SARS global outbreak was contained.
There have been no reported cases of SARS since 2004.
So patients with SARS reported high fevers and other symptoms, including headache, an
overall feeling of discomfort and body aches.
Some people also experienced mild respiratory symptoms at the outset, and 10-20% of patients
reported having diarrhea.
After 2-7 days, some SARS patients went on to develop a dry cough and most developed
pneumonia.
MERS stands for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome, and it is a viral respiratory illness first
reported in Saudi Arabia in 2012 and has since spread several other countries, including
the United States. Most people infected with MERS developed severe respiratory illness,
including fever, cough and shortness of breath. The animal source of MERS is likely to be
camels, and studies have shown that direct contact with camels is a risk factor for human
infection with MERS. However, more research is needed to understand the interactions between
humans and camels in order to get a more complete picture of how transmission takes place.
Another important piece of information is that while there are ways to test a person
for MERS and there are treatments for the disease, there is currently no vaccine available
to protect against MERS. Like MERS and SARS, the SARS-CoV-2 is a beta-coronavirus. Early
reports of the current virus linked the outbreak to a large seafood and live animal market
in China, suggesting an animal-to-person spread, later a growing number of patients reportedly
had not had contact with animal markets, marking the shift to person-to-person spread.
Person-to-person spread has been reported outside of China, including in the United
States, Japan and other countries. Most recently, other places have apparent community spread,
meaning that some people have been infected, who are not sure how or where they became
infected. While both MERS and SARS are known to cause severe illness in people, there is
still much unknown about the current virus. Symptoms of the SARS COV-2, or what many
media outlets are calling, COVID-19 virus include fever, tiredness, dry cough and shortness
of breath. Some patients also experience aches and pains, nasal congestion, runny nose,
or throat and diarrhea. It is currently believed that symptoms may appear in as few as two
days or as long as 14 days after exposure. This is based on what has been seen previously
as the incubation period of MERS. It is worth noting that while the risk of catching COVID-19,
COVID-19 from a person with no symptoms is very low, many infected people experience
only mild symptoms, particularly in the early stages of the disease.
Currently most people, about 80%, recover from the disease without needing special treatment,
but around 1 in 6 infected become seriously ill and develop difficulty breathing.
Older people and those with underlying medical problems, like high blood pressure, heart
problems or diabetes are more likely to develop serious illness. So far about 2% of people
with the disease have died. It is worth noting that this fatality rate is much lower than
that of SARS, which was estimated at 14 to 15% and then that of MERS, which has a fatality
rate of approximately 35%. However, the situation with the new virus is still evolving and
numbers may change once more data is available. Also, currently it is believed that the new
virus is much more infectious than either of the other coronaviruses that have been
spread between humans, which is part of the reason there are currently so many new cases
identified each day. As with MERS, there are currently no vaccine available. There is also
no specific antiviral medicine to prevent or treat COVID-19.
Possible vaccines and some specific drug treatments are under investigation and are being tested
through clinical trials.
